attribution: Traditionally attributed to Gautama (Akshapada); the text likely grew in layers
author: gautama-akshapada
period: Scholars place its compilation roughly between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE, with later additions possible
summary: The founding text of Nyaya: an account of the valid means of knowledge, the structure of inference, and the rules and pitfalls of debate.
whyRead: It is the foundation of Indian logic and epistemology. Almost every later school, including Buddhist and Vedantic ones, had to engage with its account of how we know.
questions: How do we know something is true?
What makes an argument valid or fallacious?
Can right knowledge lead to liberation?

keyTeachings.title: Sixteen topics
keyTeachings.text: The text opens by listing sixteen topics (padarthas), from the means of knowledge and objects of knowledge to types of debate and fallacies. Knowing them correctly is said to lead to the highest good.

keyTeachings.title: Four pramanas
keyTeachings.text: Nyaya accepts four means of valid knowledge (pramana): perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), comparison or analogy (upamana) and reliable testimony (shabda).

keyTeachings.title: The structure of inference
keyTeachings.text: Inference is set out in a five-member argument: thesis, reason, example, application and conclusion. The classic illustration is inferring fire from smoke on a hill.

keyTeachings.title: Debate and fallacies
keyTeachings.text: The text distinguishes honest discussion (vada) from debate aimed at victory (jalpa) and mere destructive criticism (vitanda). It classifies faulty reasons (hetvabhasa), quibbles and points of defeat.

keyTeachings.title: Knowledge and liberation
keyTeachings.text: Nyaya holds that false knowledge leads to faults, action, birth and suffering. Removing false knowledge through right knowledge unravels this chain and leads to liberation (apavarga).

structure.label: Five books (adhyayas), each in two sections (ahnikas)

passages.about: The sixteen topics whose true knowledge leads to the highest good
